analysis.one_liner: Slashes corporate tax rates and cuts taxes on corporate profits and investment gains.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Ways and Means Committee without ever receiving a vote after being referred there in January 2008.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the tax code in favor of corporations and investors. It would cut the top corporate income tax rate from 35% to 25%, let businesses deduct the full cost of equipment immediately instead of over time, adjust the value of stocks and property for inflation so investors pay tax only on real gains, and cut the tax rate corporations pay on capital gains from 35% to 15%. It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in January 2008 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations gain the most: every profitable corporation would pay a top rate of 25% instead of 35%, and corporate capital gains would be taxed at 15% instead of 35%. Wealthy households and other holders of stocks, real estate, and business property gain from inflation indexing, which shrinks their taxable gains the longer they hold an asset. Businesses of any size gain from unlimited immediate expensing of equipment and buildings. None of the provisions contain offsets, so the reduced revenue would be added to the deficit.

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the top corporate income tax rate from 35% to 25% by flattening the corporate rate schedule, reducing taxes for every profitable corporation.

Repeals the dollar limits on the Section 179 expensing allowance, letting businesses immediately deduct the full cost of equipment and, under the bill's text, even buildings and other real property, instead of depreciating them over years.
Adjusts the tax basis of stocks and tangible property held more than three years for inflation, so investors pay capital gains tax only on gains above the rise in the price level.
Cuts the tax rate on capital gains recognized by corporations from 35% to 15%, sharply lowering tax on corporate investment income.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury pays first, since the bill has no revenue offsets — the corporate rate cut alone is one of the largest revenue reductions available in the tax code. Over time, the cost falls on taxpayers generally through larger deficits and interest payments, and on whoever bears any future tax increases or spending cuts needed to close the gap.

drawbacks.text: The bill contained no revenue offsets: cutting the top corporate rate from 35% to 25%, cutting the corporate capital gains rate to 15%, unlimited expensing, and inflation indexing of asset basis would each reduce federal revenue, so the cost would show up as larger deficits borne by future taxpayers.

The indexing provision only applies to assets held more than three years, and only to taxpayers with written documentation of their original purchase price — so its benefits flow to longer-term holders of stocks and tangible property, a group concentrated among wealthier households, while ordinary wage earners holding few assets gain little.

Repealing the dollar limits on Section 179 expensing would let businesses of any size deduct the full cost of equipment and even real estate immediately, which simplifies tax planning but shifts more of the tax burden away from businesses and toward other taxpayers unless offset.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have delivered large, permanent tax cuts to corporations and holders of stocks and real estate, with no offsets to pay for them — meaning the cost would fall on federal borrowing and future taxpayers. Supporters argued lower rates and unlimited expensing would spur investment and growth that eventually reaches workers; the record contains no revenue estimate or analysis supporting that. The inflation-indexing provision is a genuine fix for taxing phantom gains from inflation, but because it only helps people with substantial assets held three years or more, its benefits concentrate at the top. On balance, the bill's direct benefits flowed overwhelmingly to concentrated interests, and its costs were diffuse and deferred.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on January 23, 2008 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
The action history shows no further activity after the referral — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — so the bill expired when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations and investors avoided nothing — the bill would have cut their taxes, so its death preserved existing federal revenue and left the tax burden where it was. Ordinary taxpayers are spared the deficit the unpaid-for cuts would have added.

for.name: Rep. Scott Garrett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 23, 2008 with a group of conservative House Republicans including Jim Jordan, Mike Pence, Paul Ryan, and Ron Paul.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral on January 23, 2008 — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 99 cosponsors were Republicans, and with Democrats holding the House majority in the 110th Congress, the bill never advanced past committee.

industries.note: The bill cuts the top corporate tax rate from 35% to 25% and the corporate capital gains rate from 35% to 15%, a direct, permanent reduction in taxes on corporate profits. Because the bill had no revenue offsets, the cost would fall on federal borrowing and future taxpayers.

industries.industry: Shareholders and holders of stocks, real estate, and other capital assets
industries.note: Inflation indexing of asset basis means long-term holders pay tax only on real gains above inflation, and the corporate capital gains rate drops to 15%. The benefit scales with the size of the portfolio, concentrating gains among wealthier households.

Unlimited Section 179 expensing would let any business immediately write off equipment and even buildings rather than depreciating them, improving cash flow. But the benefit tracks how much a business invests, so larger, capital-intensive firms gain the most, and the lost revenue must be made up elsewhere.
All four provisions reduce federal revenue permanently with no pay-fors in the bill. The gap would be financed by borrowing, whose interest costs are ultimately paid by taxpayers.
